query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a minor volume fraction of an oxide‐forming, self‐lubricating dispersoid phase into the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy enables in situ formation of a lubricious oxide film during sliding, thereby reducing friction and wear across a broad temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without any additional self-lubricating phase.
generation.intervention: Addition of a controlled volume fraction of an oxide‐forming dispersoid phase into the alloy during processing.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests in ambient air from room temperature to 800 °C under varying loads.
generation.structural_mediator: Under sliding conditions, the dispersoid phase oxidizes to form a stable, lubricious oxide film at the contact interface.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the formed oxide film reduces interfacial adhesion and shear, leading to lower friction and wear by acting as an in situ self-lubricant.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit lower coefficients of friction and reduced wear rates compared to the unmodified CoCrFeNi material under the tested conditions.
generation.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy that does not form a lubricious film during sliding.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective in oxygen‐rich environments, under moderate to high loads, and within the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of friction and wear improvement, particularly under the highest loads and at the extreme temperatures, remains uncertain until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one of standard CoCrFeNi alloy and one modified with the oxide‐forming dispersoid phase. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests in ambient air over the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under a series of systematically varied loads. Post-test, analyze the surface using SEM and XPS to confirm the presence and stability of the lubricious oxide film.
measurements: Coefficient of friction at various temperatures and loads
Wear rate (mass loss or wear track dimensions)
Surface composition and film morphology via SEM and XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not exhibit statistically significant reductions in friction and wear relative to the baseline, or if a stable lubricious oxide film is not confirmed by surface analyses, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor volume fraction of an oxide‐forming, self‐lubricating dispersoid phase into the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix will enable the in situ formation of a lubricious oxide film during sliding, leading to lower friction and wear rates from room temperature up to 800 °C.
drafts.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix without any additional self-lubricating phase.
drafts.intervention: Addition of a controlled volume fraction of an oxide-forming dispersoid phase into the alloy during processing.
drafts.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in ambient air over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under varying loads.
drafts.structural_mediator: The dispersoid phase oxidizes under sliding conditions to form a stable, lubricious oxide film at the sliding interface.
drafts.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the oxide-forming phase within the alloy oxidizes to form a thin, low-shear-strength film that reduces adhesion and shear at the contact surfaces. This self-generated lubricious layer effectively decreases friction and wear, while remaining active over a broad temperature range.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit significantly lower coefficients of friction and reduced wear rates compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi material, with effective performance maintained across the full temperature range, particularly at high temperatures where oxidation enhances lubrication.
drafts.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, which exhibits higher friction and wear and lacks a self-replenishing lubricious film.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective in environments where oxygen is available to support film formation, under moderate to high loads that do not exceed the stability limits of the oxide film, and within the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one set of standard CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy and one set modified with the oxide-forming dispersoid phase. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests across a controlled temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C) under a series of increasing loads in ambient air. Monitor friction coefficients and wear rates, and conduct surface analyses (e.g., XPS, SEM) to confirm the formation and stability of the oxide film.
measurements: Coefficient of friction over time at each temperature and load condition
Wear rate measurements (e.g., mass loss or wear track dimensions)
Surface chemical composition and film morphology (via XPS and SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dispersoid-enhanced alloy does not display a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear compared to the baseline alloy across the temperature and load conditions, or if no stable lubricious oxide film is observed via surface analyses, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
